title: Hugh McGary, the Blue Licks Hothead

bodyMarkdown:
Irish-born [Hugh McGary](/people/#hugh-mcgary) (1744–1806) brought his family to Kentucky in 1775 with [Daniel Boone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Boone)'s party and settled near Fort Harrod. Around 1779 he and his stepson James Ray built McGary's Station on his 400-acre settlement at Shawnee Springs, in today's Mercer County. Contemporaries described him as hot-tempered and quarrelsome; in 1781 a Mercer County court convicted him of taking bets on Sunday horse races.

On August 19, 1782, McGary was a major in the Kentucky militia at [Blue Licks](/stories/battle-of-blue-licks/). Boone urged caution at the Licking ford, but the militia crossed and walked into an ambush. A later tradition says McGary spurred into the ford shouting, "Them that ain't cowards follow me" ([HistoryNet](https://historynet.com/battle-of-blue-licks/)); it comes from recollections gathered decades afterward and is not in Boone's own 1782 or 1784 accounts. In the rout, about seventy Kentuckians died in minutes, including [Col. John Todd](/stories/col-john-todd-of-lexington/) and Israel Boone.

Four years later, on Benjamin Logan's 1786 raid on the Shawnee towns in Ohio, McGary killed the Shawnee chief [Moluntha](/stories/moluntha-and-logans-raid-1786/) after Moluntha had surrendered. A court-martial found him guilty of conduct unbecoming an officer and suspended him from command for a year.

## Kentucky today

McGary's Station is stop #65 on the James Harrod Trust's rural Mercer County driving tour, on Warwick Road near Harrodsburg.
Source: [Hugh McGary's Station (James Harrod Trust)](https://www.jamesharrodtrust.org/tours/rural-mercer-driving-tour/hugh-mcgarys-station/)
